Right whale annual detection probability in Cape Cod Bay

Source: R/data.R
ganley_detection.Rd

Table S2 of Ganley et al. (2019): goodness-of-fit p-values and average detection probability for a detection function fitted separately to each year from 1998 to 2017, from aerial line-transect surveys of Cape Cod Bay.

Usage

ganley_detection

Format

A tibble with 20 rows and 5 columns:

year

Survey year, 1998 to 2017.

cvm_p

Cramér-von Mises p-value for the year's detection function.

ks_p

Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-value.

p

Average detection probability, \(\hat{P}_a\).

p_se

Standard error of p.

Source

Ganley, L.C., Brault, S. and Mayo, C.A. (2019) What we see is not what there is: estimating North Atlantic right whale Eubalaena glacialis local abundance. Endangered Species Research 38:101-113. doi:10.3354/esr00938 , Table S2. Open access under CC-BY.

This is p, not perception

p is the average detection probability of the fitted detection function, the same quantity selection_table() reports as p (with standard error p_se). It is not a g(0) component. Ganley et al. state that perception bias was not addressed in their study, because estimating it needs a second observer team. Correcting for one while believing you have corrected for the other biases abundance by a factor. g0() names any standard component that is missing.

What it is useful for

It is a long, real example that detection probability is not a constant of a survey. Twenty years of the same programme, aircraft and bay give p between 0.431 and 0.866, with standard errors from 0.028 to 0.333.

The goodness-of-fit columns show that a model can rank well and still fail a fit test. Ganley et al. took p > 0.05 as adequate fit. 2003 fails Kolmogorov-Smirnov (0.048) but passes Cramér-von Mises (0.103), and has the largest standard error on p. This is why selection_table() reports cvm_p alongside AIC.

See also

selection_table(), ganley_availability

Examples

ganley_detection
#> # A tibble: 20 × 5
#>     year cvm_p  ks_p     p  p_se
#>    <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1  1998 0.751 0.564 0.663 0.156
#>  2  1999 0.521 0.426 0.601 0.094
#>  3  2000 0.531 0.248 0.75  0.041
#>  4  2001 0.867 0.802 0.64  0.07 
#>  5  2002 0.97  0.965 0.708 0.104
#>  6  2003 0.103 0.048 0.76  0.333
#>  7  2004 0.969 0.965 0.655 0.142
#>  8  2005 0.985 0.995 0.866 0.059
#>  9  2006 0.431 0.392 0.703 0.163
#> 10  2007 0.866 0.777 0.712 0.065
#> 11  2008 0.97  0.977 0.595 0.05 
#> 12  2009 0.581 0.507 0.591 0.038
#> 13  2010 0.668 0.785 0.599 0.046
#> 14  2011 0.847 0.737 0.604 0.043
#> 15  2012 0.991 0.982 0.611 0.062
#> 16  2013 0.98  0.993 0.576 0.03 
#> 17  2014 0.93  0.858 0.507 0.035
#> 18  2015 0.583 0.815 0.541 0.028
#> 19  2016 0.115 0.065 0.431 0.038
#> 20  2017 0.341 0.129 0.518 0.028

# Detection probability varies from year to year
range(ganley_detection$p)
#> [1] 0.431 0.866

# The year that fails Kolmogorov-Smirnov also has the least precise p
ganley_detection[ganley_detection$ks_p < 0.05, ]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>    year cvm_p  ks_p     p  p_se
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  2003 0.103 0.048  0.76 0.333
